articles.title_orig: China Truck Sales Now Majority Electric. What’s Next?
articles.title_zh: China Truck Sales Now Majority Electric. What’s Next?
articles.content_orig:
EV heavy trucks hit 50.3% market share in China for September, with sales up 34% from a year ago. Long-haul big rig market share hit 64.5%. China is on track to have over 40% EV market share for the entire year, reaching their 2030 goal in a matter of months. This is not the first time China’s heavy truck market share topped 50%, but that previous blip in December last year was prior to subsidies ending, followed by a dip in January. Current sales rates are not bolstered by the subsidy and are now on a much more stable upward trajectory.
The speed of EV adoption for heavy trucks in China has recently grown much faster than for cars, having risen from just 13.6% in 2024. When I visited Guangzhou in November of last year and again in April of this year, I noticed a lot more green plates on trucks, indicating that they were electric. It seems that my perception is backed by sales data.
With the addition of LNG trucks, diesel’s share of heavy trucks has dropped to roughly 40%. While LNG sales have also declined with the rate of EV adoption, diesel trucks could soon make up less than 1/3 of sales and decline further from there. China could feasibly double its 2030 goal and hit 80% EV penetration, by which point many diesel models are likely to be discontinued.
With these levels of market penetration, in addition to retirements, China’s diesel demand is on track to fall by about 230,000 barrels per day this year, despite increased freight movement. Every additional electric truck that replaces a diesel truck then builds on that reduction. Due to their duty cycle, each electric truck sold has a much greater impact on fuel consumption than each car sold. And the price of the fuel combined with the duty cycle has a much greater impact on overall truck economics.
To be clear, these improving results are not due to subsidies, as they appear in the year after subsidies were cut. They are also not due to mandates, as the 2030 goals were met before the ink was dry on their announcement. EV trucks are now more affordable to own and operate than diesel trucks in China. The increase in diesel prices has only increased the cost gap.
Last year, roughly 90% of all electric truck sales globally were in China. That percentage is set to expand this year, despite rising sales in some other countries. Those sales are simply not rising fast enough outside of China to keep pace with China. In comparison, the EU is looking at 2.5% EV market share this year. China is on pace to average roughly as many electric trucks sold per week as Europe sells per year. The US EV truck market looks like a rounding error in comparison at less than one percent.
In addition, China has rapidly been building out heavy truck charging infrastructure as part of the 28 million charging facilities planned to be in operation by the end of 2027, up from 21 million last March. This not only focuses on the major cities but also extends into more rural areas that have been slower to adopt electrification. In addition, several companies are building out battery swap stations. While we have yet to see if battery swap or MW+ charging wins in the truck market, expect the competition between the two approaches to be fierce.
Within Tier 1 cities, I could see a potential phase out of diesel trucks in the near future. Hainan province is already planning to end ICE passenger car sales by 2030 , and I expect that to extend to diesel trucks as well. Although rural areas have been slower to adopt, they also tend to be less wealthy and thus more impacted by the changing economics. If diesel prices stay elevated while charging becomes convenient, many rural businesses will not be able to afford to buy new diesel trucks. With the end of diesel truck sales, strict emissions standards and a potential return of scrappage incentives could take remaining diesel vehicles off the road at an accelerated rate.
With fewer diesel trucks on the road in the largest market globally, diesel consumption is set to decline. In addition, the supply chain for diesel parts will also start to decline. As protectionism has targeted electric vehicles, rather than internal combustion  engine (ICE) vehicles, a decline in Chinese (ICE) parts has a potentially significant impact on global markets.
Of course, as EVs take over the majority of heavy truck sales in the fiercely competitive Chinese market, Chinese manufacturers will start looking outside of the country for growth.
The traditional thought would be to look at wealthy Western countries that have substantial buying power. However, many Chinese companies may be a bit reluctant to focus on those markets after the protectionist efforts against electric passenger vehicles. Many European markets, like Germany, also have very high electricity prices, which makes the financial proposition less attractive for commercial vehicles that are heavily motivated by costs. Chinese companies may start focusing elsewhere.
The Middle Corridor could become a focus. This essentially rebuilds the Silk Road land route from China, across the Caspian Sea, on to Turkey. Many of the countries along this route  once had prosperous trade, only to fall into decline when ocean trade routes were established. However, land transport is much easier to electrify than long ocean voyages. China is investing heavily with countries like Kazakhstan along the route with renewable electricity infrastructure . Electrified rail is expanding by 26-fold in Turkey. Electrified trucking is the next logical step, connecting the rail lines to more local production along the route.
Other Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) countries could also benefit. In countries like Ethiopia, which has expensive diesel but electricity prices to businesses of just $0.017/kWh , electric trucks could make perfect sense to transport between new factories and new ports. Trading partners like Vietnam and Thailand could also see an influx.
All this is not to say that local companies will not benefit. Unlike passenger cars, heavy equipment tends to be more modular. Due to the bulk and mass of the vehicles, final assembly is more likely to be localized, with greater use of local suppliers.
Overall, we could see much of the “Rest of the World” (ROW) leapfrog legacy economies in EV truck adoption. The purchase price is no longer prohibitive in China, and the operating costs are much lower. With infrastructure buildout and increasing renewable installed capacity, electric trucking is poised to take over rapidly.
That is not to say that the West will be completely left out. Countries with less prohibitive trade policies toward EVs will likely see increased adoption. While EVs have taken over passenger car sales in Norway, their trucking industry still has a way to go at just 14.4%. And the geographically most eastern country typically lumped in with the “West,” Australia, is likely to see EV truck sales follow a similar pattern to EV car sales. If Canada continues to open up, they could also benefit. Of course, as the majority of the economic benefit from electric trucks comes from their use, inflated trucking costs hurt every company that moves products by truck, and those inflated costs then lead to inflation throughout the economy. That impacts overall affordability. As such, there is a chance that protectionists do not put as much effort into undermining electric truck imports as they put into passenger EVs.
And the EV heavy truck global supply chain will become increasingly well established. This could mean more parts availability for brands outside of China to build competitive vehicles, if those companies have access to global supply chains. Competitive markets will also drive innovation, moving the technology forward at an accelerating rate. Meanwhile the supply chain for diesel trucks will shrink.

articles.title_orig: Midterm election results 2026: Who’s winning and what’s at stake for stocks and the economy
articles.title_zh: Midterm election results 2026: Who’s winning and what’s at stake for stocks and the economy
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in

Control of the US Congress is the prize on November 3, 2026, as Democrats attempt to wrest majorities from President Donald Trump's Republicans in the midterm elections.
Voters will also choose governors in 36 of the 50 states, and nearly every state will hold elections for its state-level legislative bodies.
Ballots have been cast for weeks, with early voting underway across the country ahead of Election Day .
The midterms , held in the middle of each four-year presidential term, by definition do not involve the president himself.
But anyone tempted to dismiss this year's contests as lacking drama or importance should weigh two statistics.
More than 100 million people are expected to cast ballots in this year's midterm voting, if turnout is anything like the previous midterm in 2022.
And as of October 30, a record $11.6 billion had been spent on political advertisements for the 2025–26 election cycle.
AdImpact, which tracks the activities, said the top spending is in battleground US Senate races in Texas, Ohio and Michigan.
Campaign finance records show Elon Musk alone has spent $442 million to support Republicans.
Midterms generally attract fewer voters than the higher-profile presidential races.
For example, more than 155 million votes were cast in the 2024 presidential election.
In the House, Republicans currently hold a 218-214 majority, with two vacancies and one independent who caucuses with Republicans.
Democrats must win a net gain of four seats to take control of the chamber.
The Senate is also in play, where Republicans hold a 53-47 majority.
Democrats must net four additional seats to get control there.
Ten races, including those in Maine, Ohio, North Carolina, Iowa and Georgia, could decide the outcome.
Trump's approval of his performance is at an all-time low of 32 percent, according to a September Reuters/Ipsos poll.
Domestic issues like rising consumer prices are likely to affect the outcome of many races and could erode support for Republicans.
Evidence suggests Democrats are more enthusiastic about voting this year than Republicans.
If early voting trends continue, it could point to a Democratic win in November.
There are also signs that Latino voters who veered to Trump in 2024 might be returning to Democrats because of frustration over the economy and some of Trump's immigration enforcement tactics.
A landslide for the Democrats, however, is far from assured.
Republicans could benefit from continued skepticism toward Democrats, a Republican spending advantage in campaigns, and fears among moderate voters over some primary wins by left-wingers.
Midterm elections generally are dangerous territory for the political party that holds the White House and/or Congress.
For 2026, that means Trump and his Republicans controlling the US Senate and House of Representatives are in perilous political positions.
The midterms can be an opportunity for voters to, in effect, grade the president's performance, and possibly trigger White House course corrections if they receive low marks.
Midterm election results can also give aspiring presidential candidates hints on how to tailor their messages to voters in the next presidential campaign, which in this case will be in 2028.
Recent history shows the shockwaves a midterm election can produce.
In the 2010 midterms, during Barack Obama's Democratic presidency, Republicans scored major victories, winning 63 additional House seats amid an underperforming US economy and weak support for Obama's landmark healthcare reform legislation.
Democrats lost their majority.
In the Senate, they held onto control despite losing six seats.
The Republican wave was a "shellacking," Obama lamented at the time.
He subsequently faced Republican demands for significant reductions to non-defense spending.
Democrats returned the favor in 2018, with Trump in the White House.
They gained a net 40 House seats but lost a net two Senate seats.
At the state level, Republicans currently control 55% of state legislative seats across the country, while Democrats hold 43.8%, according to Ballotpedia.
If Democrats manage to win the House, the next speaker — second in line for the presidency after the vice president — is likely to be Democratic Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York.
He is currently the House Democratic leader.
Jeffries, who would become the first Black American to hold the powerful office, would be in a position to direct House committees to investigate a range of controversial activities by Trump and his associates.
Jeffries has repeatedly said Democrats would look into what he has called "unprecedented levels of corruption" during the Trump administration.
Jeffries also would steer Democrats' legislative priorities through the House.
He has said Democrats would focus on making healthcare, groceries, housing, energy and other costs more affordable.
A Republican win, on the other hand, would ensure that the speaker's gavel remains in that party's hands, either with current speaker Mike Johnson or whichever Republican prevails if he is challenged for the job.
Republican priorities are likely to be focused on additional tax cuts, huge increases in defense spending, and deeper social safety net reductions, building on Trump's 2025 "One Big Beautiful Bill."
Among the most-watched House races are Republican Representative Mike Lawler's bid for reelection to a New York district that Democratic candidate Kamala Harris won in her 2024 presidential campaign.
An open seat in a Nebraska swing district, where farmers and truckers face sharply higher fuel prices as a result of the US war against Iran, is also drawing attention.
Also high on Democrats' list of House seats they hope to take from Republicans are two in Pennsylvania and one in New Jersey.
Hovering over all of this are questions over whether Trump will try to meddle in the elections, which are administered by the 50 individual states.
Since 2020, he has repeatedly insisted there is widespread cheating in US elections, despite a lack of evidence.
State election officials and Democrats in Congress have been preparing for possible legal challenges to any moves by his administration to try to intervene.
There is no set time for when the world will learn the results of the US midterm elections.
In tight races, winners may not be called for days or even weeks.
The first individual race calls are expected to start after polls begin to close in the United States on Tuesday night, first with Indiana and Kentucky at 6 p.m. (ET) (2300 GMT).
Polls then close in Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont and Virginia at 7 p.m. (0000 GMT on November 4).
The last polls to close are in far western Alaska at 1 a.m. ET.

China is helping to train Solomon Islands police to use water cannons as part of an ongoing security partnership that is viewed with scepticism by the West.
The Chinese embassy said on Tuesday that six officers from the Royal Solomon Islands Police Force took part in a week-long training exercise, without giving dates.
The programme helped familiarise officers with the use of crowd control vehicles and different scenarios in which they may be used, the embassy said.

articles.title_orig: S&P 500 snaps 3-day skid on Election Day as chip stocks rebound
articles.title_zh: S&P 500 snaps 3-day skid on Election Day as chip stocks rebound
articles.content_orig:
With prediction markets pricing in a big victory for Democrats in Tuesday's midterm elections , traders are leaning into a group of stocks that investors often categorize as beneficiaries of left-wing leadership. Options trading in clean-energy stocks, particularly solar companies, surged on Tuesday, despite a five-month sell-off in the group that's left most of the companies in the industry group down on the year.
Follow CNBC's live coverage of the 2026 midterm elections
Volume in the Invesco Solar ETF (TAN) surged to 40 times higher than usual Tuesday, according to Cboe LiveVol data. The fund, which typically trades fewer than 500 contracts a day the past month, traded more than 20,000 contracts by midday, and 99% of them were calls. The ETF rallied more than 400% from its pandemic low through the 2020 election before giving almost all of the gains back by April last year.
The most popular trade in TAN was buying the 50-strike call for December expiry for 80 cents and looking for a 17% rally, according to SpotGamma data. For nearer expiry, the 46 and 47-strike calls were also popular. Among individual stocks, SolarEdge Technologies stands out, on pace for three times higher-than-average volume and more than 75% of trading in calls. The company reports earnings before the bell tomorrow and rallied more than 6% Tuesday. The most popular trade was buying the 35-strike call expiring Friday. "I would only like solar if blue was in the White House," said Charlie Moon of Chicago-based Prosper Trading Academy. "But Enphase does stands out with some insider buying." Bulls were indeed dabbling in Enphase Energy , whose stock fell 20% after earnings last week but have fully recovered since and rallied 9% Tuesday. On volume twice the average, traders likely bought 8,600 calls, compared to under 900 puts. The most popular trade in Enphase was to buy the 35-strike call expiring in January, a trade that costs $2.45 per contract and needs Enphase to rally 23%.

articles.title_zh: CCSU delegation visits China to celebrate legacy, education partnership with Huang
articles.content_orig:

Philanthropist C.J. Huang was honored in China.
NEW BRITAIN — A delegation from Central Connecticut State University traveled to China to celebrate philanthropist C.J. Huang’s legacy and a partnership that has connected students and teachers from both countries for more than 35 years.
The delegation visited Hengdong County, China to mark the 110th anniversary of Huang’s birth and the 40th anniversary of Ouyang Yu Experimental Middle School, which he helped build.
According to the university, Carmen Veloria, associate vice president for academic affairs, and Xudong Jia, dean of the School of Engineering, Science and Technology, represented CCSU during an Oct. 2 ceremony.
“As we honor this history, we look ahead. Central will deepen this partnership — in student exchange, faculty collaboration and emerging fields like artificial intelligence, robotics and cybersecurity. More than 35 years ago, Mr. Huang built a bridge between our communities; our responsibility now is to keep it strong for a new generation,” Veloria said.
The partnership began in 1990 when Huang established a scholarship program allowing students from Ouyang Yu to attend CCSU and university graduate students to teach English in China.
Since then, 12 teachers and 22 graduates from the Chinese school have studied at CCSU. Another student arrived this fall. The school has also welcomed 57 international teachers, including 18 connected to CCSU.
Born in China in 1916, Huang became a successful businessman and supported projects in education, science, and medicine. CCSU awarded him an honorary Doctor of Humane Letters degree in 1990.
Before his death in 2012, Huang left $6.5 million to CCSU for scholarships and a new recreation center.
According to the university, the 58,000-square-foot C.J. Huang Recreation Center opened in January 2020. It includes basketball courts, fitness rooms and an indoor running track.
His wife, Ha-Lin Huang, and daughters, Sheila Li and Alice Mark, visited the university in 2023 to see the facility and attend a private ceremony honoring his contributions.
CCSU also maintains scholarship funds bearing Huang’s name, including one supporting educational exchanges with the Chinese school.

articles.title_orig: Canva is announcing changes and layoffs affecting 22 percent of its staff
articles.title_zh: Canva is announcing changes and layoffs affecting 22 percent of its staff
articles.content_orig:
Some Canva workers may have different roles, be asked to relocate, or be laid off.
Some Canva workers may have different roles, be asked to relocate, or be laid off.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Canva is making significant changes affecting 1,271 people, which is 22 percent of its staff, co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins announced today . “For some people, this will mean changes to their roles or being asked to relocate to centralised hubs,” says Perkins. “Sadly, it will also mean saying goodbye to teammates and friends who have helped build Canva into what it is today.”
In her note to staff, Perkins says that:
After exploring a wide range of alternatives, I’ve come to the difficult conclusion that small changes won’t be enough. To set ourselves up for the next decade, we need to refound Canva, getting back to our roots of small, empowered teams with the freedom to make decisions, take ownership and focus on what matters most for our community.
Canva’s changes include bringing its Product, Growth, and Platform teams together into one product organization, “simplifying layers” and “consolidating overlapping responsibilities,” and making Sydney the “primary home for more of our product teams, as well as roles in other Specialties where shared context and close collaboration are especially important.” Starting in January, Canva will also “expect” most hybrid employees to spend 2 to 3 days in an office each week “depending on what makes sense in your area.”
Employees leaving Canva will get benefits including at least six months of salary, twelve months of healthcare coverage, and career support resources.
Yesterday, Squarespace announced layoffs affecting 19 percent of its staff .

articles.title_orig: Google Curbs AI in School Accounts After Pushback
articles.title_zh: Google Curbs AI in School Accounts After Pushback
articles.content_orig:
We’re bringing Guided Learning capabilities to Search and Google Classroom, and evolving our approach to school controls.
VP & General Manager, Education
Your browser does not support the audio element.
Chris Phillips, VP and General Manager of Education, is introducing Guided Learning to Google Search and Google Classroom to help students think critically through complex problems. These tools provide step-by-step coaching instead of direct answers to support productive study habits. You can find Guided Learning in Google Classroom today, and we are beginning a pilot program for Search in select U.S. schools later this month.
Chris Phillips, VP and General Manager of Education, explains that we are adding Guided Learning to Google Search and Classroom to help students think through problems instead of just finding quick answers. This tool acts like a personal coach, using questions to guide students through complex topics step by step. We are also giving school administrators full control to decide which AI tools are available to their students, ensuring technology supports classroom learning.
If you’ve ever watched a student use AI tools to help with their schoolwork, you’ve probably wondered: Are they actually learning, or just finding a shortcut? Questions like this are important, and they guide our work when building products for learning.
We believe technology paired with great educators can unlock incredible learning potential, and we’re focused on building technology responsibly to help students thrive. Today, we’re making important updates to our products used in schools, including building Guided Learning capabilities into Google Search and Google Classroom, and evolving our approach to school controls.
We believe AI products should support “productive struggle” — enabling students to be actively challenged without getting so overwhelmed that they give up. That’s the philosophy behind Guided Learning. In Gemini, Guided Learning acts as an interactive study tool that coaches students through the process of problem solving through open-ended questions and step-by-step breakdowns. Our research shows that Guided Learning leads to measurable learning gains for students, and we’re now bringing Guided Learning to more products.
Google Classroom: Starting today, Guided Learning is globally available in Google Classroom, a central hub where teachers and students organize schoolwork, share assignments and stay connected. When a student starts a Guided Learning activity assigned by their teacher, it acts like a 1-1 study tool, anchored in class material to help them stay on task. It also gives teachers real-time insights to spot where the class might need extra support.
Before launching Guided Learning in Google Classroom, we worked closely with schools and educators to test the feature and integrate their feedback.
We believe schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and in providing administrators with controls to help them manage their approach. After listening to schools, teachers, leading researchers, and policymakers, we are now updating our approach to controls for Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search. Access to these products will be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until school administrators explicitly turn them on.
We’ll share more specifics with schools in the coming months ahead of the changes rolling out so they have time to prepare and enable a smooth transition. Our goal is simple: provide school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products in classrooms as they see fit.
We’ll continue to listen to feedback and evolve our approach as we work in partnership with schools, teachers, pedagogical experts, and parents on helping the next generation learn and thrive.

articles.title_orig: How Wall Street analysts think the midterms could affect the stock market
articles.title_zh: How Wall Street analysts think the midterms could affect the stock market
articles.content_orig:
The midterm elections could reshape Congress as lawmakers grapple with persistent inflation , high energy prices and rising fiscal debt . For investors, by contrast, the political outcome could deliver a boost.
Data from financial firm Edward Jones shows that the S&P 500 stock index rose an average of 1.7% in the month after the last 14 midterm races, dating back to 1970. In the six months following midterm elections, S&P returns averaged 15.5%.
"Volatility around the vote is possible, but markets have historically performed well in the year following midterms as political uncertainty recedes and attention returns to the economic outlook," Magdalena Ocampo, market strategist at the global investment firm Principal Asset Management, said in an email on Tuesday as Americans cast their votes.
With congressional control in the balance, Wall Street analysts are also considering the impact divided government could have on stocks if the Democrats win the House, Senate or both chambers. Political gridlock has historically been good for markets because it limits Congress' ability to pass sweeping tax and spending legislation, reducing the risk of volatility, according to analysts.
"Less change makes a more predictable environment, which allows companies to invest in longer-term projects," Chris Low, chief economist at FHN Financial, a capital markets firm, said in an email Tuesday. "That tends to be good for earnings."
Less stock market volatility doesn't guarantee investors an easy ride, however. Gridlock in Washington, D.C., could also fuel another partisan standoff on the nation's debt, which recently surpassed $40 trillion , or spur the U.S. government to increase its borrowing to fund its priorities, according to economists.
That could unnerve bond investors, who are worried that Washington is on an unsustainable fiscal trajectory, Ed Yardeni, president of Yardeni Research, said in a note to investors.
"Prolonged shutdowns and fiscal standoffs could push Treasury yields higher, weighing on equity valuations," he said.
The Bipartisan Policy Center, a Washington, D.C.-based think tank, estimates that the U.S. will reach the debt limit again sometime between late winter and midsummer of 2027. At that point, lawmakers will have to decide whether to raise the debt ceiling, temporarily suspend it or risk another government shutdown.
Volatility could also persist if President Trump continues to rely on his executive authority to accomplish his priorities, Yardeni said. In that case, Democrats would have little power to restrain Mr. Trump even if they controlled Congress, he noted.
"Hence, a blue wave could deliver a cold shower for stocks, though we would view a significant selloff as a buying opportunity given the remarkable strength of the economy and corporate earnings," Yardeni said.
A Democratic sweep could have other implications for the economy beyond financial markets. That could include Democrats blocking Trump-appointed regulators, according to Jaret Seiberg, a financial policy analyst and managing director at investment bank TD Cowen.
"They [could] leverage this power to force the President to fill Democratic seats on independent agencies like the FDIC, SEC and CFTC," he said.
A Democratic majority in the Senate would also elevate Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, to head the Senate Banking Committee, giving her more latitude to pass populist legislation, Seiberg added. Warren would replace South Carolina Republican Sen. Tim Scott, who currently chairs the influential panel.

articles.title_orig: How malware and a bogus job interview let attackers nab $6.3B from Binance
articles.title_zh: How malware and a bogus job interview let attackers nab $6.3B from Binance
articles.content_orig:
Hackers, widely believed to be from North Korea, duped a Binance engineer into downloading malicious software that allowed them to pull off a $6.3 billion cyber heist of the crypto exchange. Dan Kitwood/Getty Images Europe hide caption
The massive $6.3 billion cyber heist suffered by crypto exchange Binance last week may have taken place in only about twenty minutes — but the attacks were months in the making.
That's according an initial assessment released by Binance on Tuesday about how it suffered the world's biggest-ever cyber heist by hackers the FBI has identified as being a North Korean state-sponsored unit.
Those findings show the hackers first tried testing and penetrating Binance's security systems back in June, though the crypto exchange was able to detect that attempt and stop it.
Though unsuccessful, that attempt allowed the hackers — identified by the FBI as a North Korean military unit called TraderTraitor — to learn more about Binance and its systems.
Then, the hackers tried again. In September, a Binance engineer was contacted in a job-hunting platform by a person posing as a "project director" from a company that turned out to be fictious.
The engineer then conducted a first-round interview with a supposed HR representative from the fake company. The hackers used this interview to "build trust," with the Binance employee, the exchange said. The interviewer even shared supposed social media accounts, as well as personal photos and videos with the Binance engineer.
"This was more advanced and deceptive than previously seen social engineering approaches," Binance said in its assessment.
The engineer was then told he would be conducting a second interview with the supposed CEO of the company in a popular social chat app. It was in this interview that the Binance employee — who was at his work laptop — was asked to download "an assignment" as part of the job recruitment process.
Instead, the "assignment" contained malicious code that allowed hackers to build out an attack that culminated last week when hackers made off with over $6 billion worth of crypto currencies held by Binance's customers at the exchange.
Binance said in the statement posted on X that the company is taking a series of actions, including an independent cybersecurity review to prevent future attacks. On Monday the exchange had said it had already replaced most of the stolen crypto currencies stolen by customers using its own funds.
"This should not have happened," Binance said in its assessment on Tuesday. "And we apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry."

US stocks were mixed as Americans went to the polls for the midterm elections and braced for more earnings from the AI industry, including chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD ).

This evening, investors will watch the election results and ballot initiatives for insights into potential policy changes on key issues affecting markets, including pharmaceuticals, the housing market, and AI data centers.
But before then, AMD will report earnings after the closing bell, giving investors another glimpse of AI demand at a precarious time for the artificial intelligence trade. As Intel's ( INTC ) stock demonstrated last week , the market's reaction is likely to depend as much on Q4 guidance as on the company's top- and bottom-line results in the most recent quarter.
Apple ( AAPL ) stock fell following its own earnings report, which showed several bright spots (iPhone sales) but also some misses (Greater China revenue). Palantir ( PLTR ) stock also fell post-earnings despite results that beat expectations.
While earnings season continues apace, the Labor Department released its monthly Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) report, showing openings and hiring changed little in September, continuing the labor market's "low hire, low fire" trend.

The major averages diverged as Americans headed to the polls to vote for congressional seats and state policies across the US.
Oil prices trimmed losses by afternoon trading on Tuesday. Brent crude futures ( BZ=F ) dropped less than 1% to hover near $104 per barrel, while WTI ( CL=F ) exchanged hands near $96 per barrel.

Data center infrastructure company Super Micro ( SMCI ) will report its fiscal first-quarter earnings after the bell on Tuesday, as the AI trade attempts a comeback following sharp declines driven by renewed fears of an AI bubble.

Hackers behind the record-breaking Binance heist spent weeks masquerading as recruiters and faux executives, eventually convincing an engineer to download malicious software onto a work computer as part of a larger-scale ruse, the company said Tuesday.
Binance said the ploy included two rounds of interviews, with a supposed HR representative conducting the first interview and sharing their social media account information to gain trust with the programmer. A second person, posing as the CEO of a fake company, later convinced the engineer to download a file containing malware under the guise of an interview assessment.
The fake job interview was just one stage of the hackers' multistep attack. Binance said the campaign began in June when another engineer downloaded a tampered software installer. Additional employee devices were compromised before the hackers gained access to systems involved in authorizing wallet transactions.
Over the weekend, the Federal Bureau of Investigation said Democratic People's Republic of Korea was behind the incident. The rogue regime has since denied the allegation.
Binance added in the update that it has fended off 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threat cases so far this year.

The value of the crypto market rose slightly Tuesday to $2.6 trillion, but the industry's near-term direction heading into November looks far from clear.

articles.title_orig: House Republicans accuse the American Psychological Association of antisemitism, threaten accreditation
articles.title_zh: House Republicans accuse the American Psychological Association of antisemitism, threaten accreditation
articles.content_orig:
An accreditation crisis gives the American Psychological Association a unique opportunity to restore scientific integrity and evidence-based practice over ideology.
Photo: J Studios/DigitalVision via Getty Images
The American Psychological Association, the nation’s largest professional organization for psychologists, could lose its power to accredit educational programs. In late September, a key federal oversight board voted to recommend suspending the APA as a federal accreditor. If the Secretary of Education accepts the recommendation, the APA will lose its status for the first time in the organization’s history.
The vote followed “scathing” third-party comments from practicing psychologists and policy professionals. Critics charged the APA with politicizing its programs, including the embrace of “ critical ” psychotherapies that make dubious assumptions about “gender identity” and label Jews colonial oppressors. The APA’s commitment to social-justice ideology undermines its program quality and nondiscrimination standards , commenters noted , particularly in its failure to address complaints of anti-Semitism.
Finally, a reason to check your email.
Sign up for our free newsletter today.
These issues are just part of a broader pattern of decline. As Manhattan Institute Senior Fellow Colin Wright and Andrew Hartz recently reported , roughly 70 of the 90 panels at a 2026 APA conference had clear ideological agendas, including “loosening/abolishing gender assessment guidelines” for medical transition. The APA also recently elected Candice Hargons—a psychologist who campaigned on a commitment to “dismantle oppressive systems” and dismissed “objectivity” as an enemy of scientific integrity—as its next president.
While the APA’s Commission on Accreditation disagreed with the oversight board’s recommendation, it vowed to address all the issues raised in its hearing and to bring itself into compliance with federal regulations . Taking the Commission at its word, the possible suspension represents a rare opportunity for the APA to reinvigorate its standards and rebuild its organizational culture to promote the interests of psychology trainees and the public they serve—not social-justice ideology.
How can the APA turn its ship around? Some basic reforms include introducing a scientific integrity standard, definitions for what constitutes “unsettled” scientific areas, a revised “non-discrimination” standard, and clearer protocols for navigating program complaints.
First, the APA should recommit itself to open scientific inquiry on controversial issues like gender medicine. That would mean adding “scientific integrity” to its enumerated professional values for accredited programs. Doing so would help ensure that APA-accredited programs create environments where faculty and students can teach and research competing scientific viewpoints in good faith.
Currently, the APA dismisses solid criticism of the weak evidence base for youth gender medicine—which prompted medical practice reversals in countries that had been early adopters—as “ misinformation .” That has to change. Greater tolerance is also needed for research findings that challenge the affirming model of care or the supposed immutability of “gender identity.” Committing the organization to a single approach to treating gender dysphoria renders psychologists ill-equipped to navigate the psychological and developmental nuance required to work with today’s gender-confused youth.
Second, the Commission could introduce benchmarks for what constitutes “contested or unsettled” scientific areas. While the APA requires programs to demonstrate alignment with “the current evidence base” across psychological competencies, its public claims regarding the benefits of youth gender medicine are often based on cherry-picked individual studies that don’t reflect the findings of systematic reviews of evidence that evaluate overall evidence quality. Clear benchmarks would build on the scientific integrity standard by requiring programs to disclose the certainty of the evidence and present credible, competing interpretations where there is disagreement.
The change would benefit the APA by eliminating ambiguity—for example, by defining “unsettled” as open questions about benefits and risks according to the findings of systematic reviews, or when reputable clinical practice guidelines recommend varying approaches to the same issue. Clear benchmarks here would benefit trainees and the Commission, while also protecting the APA reputationally.
A related change would be to make it clear that the organization’s resolutions, testimony, and position statements are not proxies for scientific validity —a use to which they are often put. Nor should deviations from the APA’s conclusions automatically demonstrate an APA program’s noncompliance. The Commission should also consider explicitly distinguishing between advocacy positions and empirical findings through the use of evidence hierarchies .
Psychology students deserve equal treatment and access to APA programs. But the Commission’s “DEI” standards go much further than this guarantee. They would be more effective if presented in the language of a universal, nondiscrimination standard. The APA should not require trainees to agree with their philosophical claims about demographic characteristics like “gender identity.”
Addressing the Commission’s concerns about anti-Semitism poses a different challenge. While APA standards ostensibly already protect Jewish students, explicitly extending these protections to secular Jews is worth considering.
The APA’s anti-Semitism issues, however, are arguably more the result of insufficient enforcement than of inadequate protections. Moreover, the code of federal regulations governing accreditation already requires accreditors to review standards-related complaints—including complaints of anti-Semitism—fairly and promptly.
Clearer timelines for resolving complaints would help, as would establishing formal corrective actions for when programs refuse to investigate credible, standards-related complaints. The Commission could also strengthen existing recordkeeping requirements for how programs assess and resolve such issues, including documenting any corrective measures taken.
If the Commission on Accreditation is serious about the government’s concerns, these recommendations are low-hanging fruit. These revised standards are already consistent with the values and spirit of existing accreditation standards and would buttress them in ways that are aligned with the Commission’s quality standards and emphasis on education that serves the interests of patients and future psychologists.
In an era defined by public distrust in institutions, the APA has a rare opportunity to stand up for scientific integrity, evidence-based practice, and equal access. For the sake of patients and trainees, let’s hope that it seizes it.
Joseph Figliolia is a policy analyst at Manhattan Institute.

Video captures the moment two helicopters collide while trying to land at Pheriche Helipad in Nepal and the aftermath of the deadly accident.
Two helicopters collided while attempting to land just below Mount Everest base camp in Nepal.
The accident happened at about 8:12 a.m. Tuesday in the Pheriche area of Solukhumbu District, according to a translated press release from the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal (CAAN). The helicopters were identified as an Air Dynasty aircraft and a Fishtail Air aircraft, the aviation authority said.
Two foreign tourists were aboard the Fishtail Air helicopter. One of them, 47-year-old Vasanth Kumar Balaramudu of Chennai, India, died in the accident, according to CAAN.
DEADLY HELICOPTER CRASH KILLS 2 PILOTS BATTLING RAGING WILDFIRE IN YOSEMITE
The other tourist, New Zealand national Shailesh Kisan Patel, was injured, along with at least one pilot involved in the collision, the authority said.
Those injured in the collision were admitted to a hospital in Kathmandu for further treatment, according to the aviation authority.
The two helicopters pictured above collided while attempting to land just below Mount Everest base camp in Nepal. (Reuters)
CAAN has opened an investigation into the accident and will determine whether corrective action is needed based on its findings.
Fishtail Air said its helicopter crashed during landing while transporting passengers rescued from the Everest region , Reuters reported.

The Air Dynasty helicopter was carrying only cargo, an official with the company told Reuters.
Helicopters are a key form of transportation around Everest, where there are no roads. They are used to evacuate trekkers and guides suffering from illness or exhaustion amid the region's cold temperatures and high altitude, according to The Associated Press (AP).
The two helicopters shown above collided with each other while attempting to land near Mount Everest base camp in Nepal. (Viral Press)
Pheriche, where the accident occurred, sits about 13,780 feet above sea level and is located below Everest base camp, the AP reported.
The collision also came after heavy snow had covered trekking routes in the region.
Conditions improved Sunday, allowing thousands of trekkers to begin moving through the area again, according to the outlet.

In September, about 70 Americans remained unaccounted for following catastrophic flooding along the Nepal-China border, while 18 Americans had been confirmed safe, Fox News Digital previously reported.
A damaged helicopter sits after two helicopters collided as they prepared to land in Nepal's Mount Everest region on Nov. 3, 2026. (Reuters)
The flooding was triggered by an Aug. 26 glacier collapse and caused widespread destruction, including flash floods and landslides. Rescue crews were searching areas, including hydropower project tunnels, where workers were believed to be trapped.

articles.title_orig: AMD beats Q3 estimates, as data center revenue climbs 97%
articles.title_zh: AMD beats Q3 estimates, as data center revenue climbs 97%
articles.content_orig:
Advanced Micro Devices reported third-quarter earnings on Tuesday that beat Wall Street's expectations, with revenue jump 45% and data center sales nearly doubling from a year earlier. The stock jumped 7% in extended trading.
Here's how the chipmaker did versus LSEG consensus estimates for the quarter:
Revenue increased from $9.25 billion a year earlier, AMD said in a statement .
CEO Lisa Su said in a press release that she expects growth in data center processors to "accelerate further," and that meeting demand won't be a problem.
"With our leadership product portfolio and deep customer and supply chain relationships, we are confident in our ability to sustain very strong revenue growth and expanding profitability over the coming years " Su said in a statement.
AMD's report comes days after Intel disclosed similar data center growth, with revenue in that segment up 78% in the third quarter. But the stock plummeted 29% on Friday over concerns about weak guidance and Intel's ability to meet demand .
The data center unit makes up the majority of AMD's business, accounting for 64% of overall revenue, up from 47% a year ago.
After years spent chasing Nvidia in the market for artificial intelligence graphics processing units, or GPUs, AMD's central processing units, or CPUs, are experiencing a major resurgence with the rise of agentic AI apps like Meta 's Muse. AMD's server CPUs are key for agentic apps because they power virtual machines and can run for hours on their own. Demand from agentic AI boosted AMD shares to a record in October.
AMD's stock is up about 125% this year, but it saw three consecutive days of losses before rallying on Tuesday amid an industrywide sell-off tied to fears about overspending on AI.
AMD is also a major player the in weakening PC market, which Intel blamed for its poor outlook last week. AMD and Intel are the largest makers of traditional x86 processors that power many laptops and desktops, while other laptops rely on Arm -based processors from the likes of Qualcomm and Apple.
Global PC shipments declined 4% in the second quarter from a year earlier due to soaring costs for memory and other components, according to Counterpoint Research .
AMD reports PC chip sales in a segment combined with gaming chips. Revenue in that business fell 8% from a year earlier to $3.7 billion. Gaming revenue was down 40% from a year ago.
For the fourth quarter, AMD said it expects about $17 billion in revenue, beating the $16.2 billion average analyst estimate, according to LSEG. AMD sees its gross margin for the quarter coming in at 55%, slightly below the average estimate of 55.3%, according to StreetAccount.
AMD also sells data center GPUs and full rack-scale systems called Helios that compete directly with Nvidia's Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin. Meta, Microsoft , Anthropic, OpenAI, and Oracle are all beginning to use AMD Helios in their data centers. Meta said last week that its Helios racks are up and running, and AMD agreed to invest $1 billion in Meta's equity offering.
AMD has also committed to investing up to $5 billion in Anthropic, which unveiled its highly anticipated prospectus last week as it inches closer to a potentially historic initial public offering .
During a visit to Taiwan in October, Su said she plans to "substantially increase our supply in 2027." Su and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang have both made multiple trips to Taiwan and South Korea this year, holding meetings with key suppliers like Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and memory leaders SK Hynix and Samsung.
In September, AMD said it would acquire World Labs for $8.2 billion in an all-stock deal. The San Francisco-based AI lab, founded by industry pioneer Fei-Fei Li, is developing a so-called world model that simulates 3D environments to aid in developing robots and other physically grounded AI applications.

articles.content_orig:
In addition to the new app icon , Google Messages is testing a redesign of pinned chats and search on the homepage.
Instead of pinned chats just appearing at the top of the list, Google Messages is trying a redesign that significantly elevates them above all conversations.
This redesign takes advantage of the existing background layer that’s currently just home to the logo/wordmark, search, and account menu.
You’ll see large contact photos appear above all chats, which pushes the list of other conversations down the page. Like iMessage on iOS, this layout has the downside of not showing any history or last sent information.
Meanwhile, Google is testing another change where search becomes a centered floating action button (FAB) alongside new chat. When you’re scrolling down the page, you’ll see “Search” in a pill-shaped button, with the other button minimized.
Otherwise, you’ll see a circular magnifying glass icon and “Start chat” in the pill. The animation that accompanies this change looks nice and feels alive.
This is a nice change for one-handed usage. It’s unclear if Google is removing the Gemini FAB with this update.
These updates are currently in the beta channel and not yet widely rolled out to testers.

articles.title_zh: Hiding inside Palantir’s skyrocketing quarter is a foreboding signal
articles.content_orig:
Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.
Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.
The data analysis company Palantir delivered such a huge third-quarter earnings report on Monday that its press release even bragged that the numbers were “crushing consensus expectations.”
Yet retail investors were lukewarm on the company on Tuesday, with the stock trading slightly down. That’s because Palantir’s enterprise sales, its big growth area, showed signs of slowing.
First, the good news for the company’s investors. Revenue grew 96% from a year earlier, and 20% from the previous quarter, to $2.31 billion, beating analysts’ expectations of $2.18 billion. It was the first time Palantir has topped $2 billion in a quarter. Palantir also reported adjusted earnings per share (profit per share, excluding certain one-time items) of 44 cents, compared with analysts’ expectations of 41 cents. The company even raised its revenue guidance, or forecast, for the full year. Normally, that alone would send a stock soaring.
The clincher was that Palantir’s U.S. commercial revenue surpassed U.S. government revenue for the first time ever. The company reported $984 million in commercial contracts (up 148% from the year-ago quarter), versus $953 million in U.S. government revenue.
The reason for all this love from enterprises? They are signing up for the company’s AI software that can run frontier models and custom-train open-weight models securely, without sharing any of their data and business processes with outside AI labs. Plus, Palantir has long offered what is today known as “forward-deployed” software engineering, in which its own engineers work directly with customers to customize the software.
However, Palantir also revealed a less-than-rosy signal: Even as enterprises are moving faster than ever, they are often signing short-term trials.
“What Ryan and I are seeing on the front line and commercial is this much quicker interaction, much quicker to deployment, shorter duration of the contract but then an ability to expand that contract dramatically,” CEO Alex Karp (pictured above) told Wall Street analysts on the quarterly earnings call.
Palantir is experiencing one of the unique phenomena of AI in the enterprise right now. Corporations are willing to quickly try AI software, skipping the usual bureaucracy, but they are also more willing to cancel contracts.
Karp used one off-color metaphor after another to describe how unconcerned he was about holding onto his enterprise business.
“We’ve gone from being the most attractive person in the physics department to being the captain of the football team, kind of thing,” he said, describing the influx of prospective corporate customers flowing in. “Conversely, you know, once you go Palantir, you don’t go back, and that’s just how it is, and you see it in our numbers.”
The numbers don’t yet confirm Palantir’s long-term success. While the company closed a hefty $1.46 billion of total contract value from U.S. enterprises in the quarter, that’s actually a decline from the record $2.13 billion in the previous quarter. That suggests slowing sales, at least in the most recent quarter.
The next earnings will show whether Palantir has solidified its role as a rising U.S. enterprise AI provider. Historically, many enterprises sign their biggest tech purchases in the final quarter of the year. Karp and his team certainly sound confident. They increased guidance for U.S. commercial revenue to be “in excess of $3.559 billion, representing a growth rate of at least 143%.”

articles.title_orig: Xbox’s Arkane Studios Attracts Multiple Bidders, Including Ubisoft
articles.title_zh: Xbox’s Arkane Studios Attracts Multiple Bidders, Including Ubisoft
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft intends to divest from Dishonored and Marvel's Blade developer Arkane Studios as part of its mass layoffs at Xbox and other Microsoft divisions. Because Arkane is based in Lyon, France, Xbox has had to adhere to French labor laws, and was mandated to search for a potential buyer for Arkane.
Assassin's Creed maker Ubisoft has reportedly made an offer for Arkane, Bloomberg reported on Tuesday. Ubisoft is one of at least three companies to submit a bid for Arkane. According to Bloomberg, Xbox is also considering selling Arkane to the studio's management.
The future of Arkane looked in doubt last month as negotiations for a redundancy plan for potentially laid-off employees were reportedly not going well ahead of a Nov. 13 deadline. That deadline for Arkane to find a new home was extended , and Xbox is "exploring options" for what to do with Arkane ahead of its December deadline, Bloomberg said. Xbox has not accepted any offer at this time.
Marvel's Blade was announced almost three years ago at the 2023 The Game Awards . Arkane has been quiet about it since, and its internal ship date was delayed until late 2027 .
If Arkane avoids being shut down by Microsoft and gets sold elsewhere, it will likely be able to wrap up development on its game starring The Daywalker. According to Bloomberg, Blade is "expected to be released within the next year or two."
Blade is a fan-favorite Marvel character who's a dhampir, a hybrid of a vampire and a human. He's appeared in Marvel's Midnight Suns , Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls , Marvel Rivals , and more.

articles.title_orig: Spanish transport minister resigns after two deadly train crashes in one year
articles.title_zh: Spanish transport minister resigns after two deadly train crashes in one year
articles.content_orig:
Spain’s Minister of Transport Óscar Puente announced his resignation after two deadly train crashes occurred in a single year, including one last week that killed 69 people and injured more than 200.
“I made the decision about my future in the first few minutes after the tragedy,” Puente told lawmakers in Madrid. “A transport minister in a country like Spain cannot remain in office after two accidents of this severity in less than a year, however different they may be and regardless of whether or not they bear direct responsibility for them.”
Puente resigned six days after one train plowed into another after what authorities say was a combination of human and computer errors along a high speed railway line connecting Madrid and Andalusia. One train, operated by Spain’s national rail service, crashed into a stationary train at high speed during a safety system failure that had halted all rail traffic along the line.
“There was a red signal prohibiting movement, yet the train was authorized to proceed,” Puente said last week. “It is a decision made under inexplicable circumstances.”
Last week’s crash was preceded by another serious rail accident in January, where two high-speed trains collided head-on in the town of Adamuz, killing at least 41 people. At the time, it was the deadliest crash Spain had seen in more than a decade.
Numerous politicians and Spain’s transport workers’ union had called on Puente to resign in the aftermath of last week’s collision. The night of the crash, police scuffled with a hundreds of protesters outside the transport ministry headquarters, some of whom carried placards demanding that Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez resign.
Puente’s announcement arrives just three weeks before the country’s general elections, in which the minister said he would not be standing as a candidate. Sánchez called those elections early in the wake of several corruption scandals, a controversy over housing affordability and numerous setbacks for his socialist PSOE party in municipal elections.
Sánchez praised Puente in a statement on social media, saying that the former transport minister stepped aside “out of respect for the victims and the progressive project.”
“Politicians like him dignify our country and show us that not all of us are the same,” Sánchez wrote. “While some only give lessons, others give everything.”

articles.title_orig: King calls slave trade a 'shameful chapter' during Commonwealth address
articles.title_zh: King calls slave trade a 'shameful chapter' during Commonwealth address
articles.content_orig:
King Charles has described the transatlantic slave trade as a "shameful chapter of history" that filled him with "profound sorrow" as he opened a summit of Commonwealth leaders in the Caribbean.
He said the trade in enslaved persons "still casts a shadow" over the association of nations.
There have been calls from some for the UK to make a formal apology for its historic role in the slave trade ahead of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda, but there was not one in the King's address.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham, also at the summit, has said that he is open to Britain issuing a formal apology but has ruled out financial reparations.
While there was no direct apology, the King did offer some contrition - and there was also an acknowledgement that he had personally learnt more about the legacy of the slave trade.
He said: "The transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands and other members of our Commonwealth.
"As I have said before, that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow."
He told the summit: "The more I have furthered my own understanding of the issues, through listening, learning and looking, the more committed I have become to finding ways for us to work in modern partnership to address the wrongs of the past with action for the future."
King Charles continued: "History is not ours to choose or to change. It is bequeathed to us in complex synthesis by forebears we can never know.
"Our inheritance includes both their achievements and their failures – the good they did as well as the wrongs."
The King's address also referenced the "brutal conflicts" the world is facing, the "catastrophic reality" of climate and rapid technological development.
The Chogm meeting gathers leaders from 56 states every two years in a different part of the Commonwealth, a voluntary grouping made up primarily of former territories of the British Empire.
The biennial meeting's official theme this year is Accelerating Partnerships and Investment for a Prosperous Commonwealth.
Speaking on Tuesday, Burnham said his government was bringing a new approach, aiming to "revitalise the Commonwealth", despite turning down demands for reparations.
"I've been very clear that we do not support reparations," he said.
"But it's not the case that we don't support countries in the Commonwealth around development, and helping them with debt issues that they've got, green finance.
"That's what we've done under all governments and in my view we should continue to do as part of being a Commonwealth."
The King and Queen are on a tour of the Caribbean which has reignited difficult debates over the UK's colonial legacy in the region.
On his first stop in the Bahamas, the King delivered a speech in which he spoke of the "suffering of the past".
In Guyana, he visited the site of a Slave Rebellion, where hundreds of enslaved people were killed.

Cyril Widdershoven is a senior maritime, energy, and geopolitical analyst and Senior Advisor at Blue Water Strategy, specialising in the strategic intersection of shipping, ports,…
The world’s largest listed oil company, Saudi Aramco, is again in the spotlight. The company’s results, released on 3 November, clearly offer an uncomfortable lesson in wartime economics. Yes, an oil company can post higher profits even as its physical operating position deteriorates. Higher prices can counter lost production; exceptional accounting gains can lift headline earnings. Still, none of these proves the underlying business is secure.
Aramco reported third-quarter net income of $36.25 billion, up 34.5% year-on-year. However, adjusted net income rose about 9% to $31.20 billion, while declining 6.6% from Q2. While the headline suggests acceleration, adjusted figures only show a business benefiting from expensive oil while confronting substantial constraints.
The question is not whether Aramco is profitable, but whether those profits can sustainably finance shareholder distributions, domestic investment, international market access, and a more resilient export system. These facts matter as Saudi Arabia’s fiscal demands continue rising.
Earnings deserve scrutiny at present. Aramco’s September exit from the Malaysian PRefChem joint ventures has generated a $6.91 billion gain. Its interim report explains that this included derecognition of net liabilities and recognition of additional receivables associated with crude supplied. Total PRefChem trade receivables at closing were $7.33 billion. Around $1.55 billion has been received, with the remainder to be settled over six years. Clearly not a $6.91 billion cash windfall.
The above explains how to read all. Accounting gains are legitimate but should not be read as having the same recurring value as cash earned from producing and selling oil. It also does not show that international integration invariably delivers attractive returns. The only outcome is that portfolio discipline sometimes requires retreat.
Cash flow also raises another warning. Q3 free cash flow exceeded quarterly base distributions. However, over the last nine months, free cash flow of $59.10 billion remained below base dividends paid of $65.66 billion. Free cash flow has increased by only 2% despite a much stronger realized oil price.
There is no liquidity crisis, but internally generated cash after capital expenditures did not fully fund base shareholder distributions over that period. Other demands have come from acquisitions and other cash commitments. Yes, low gearing provides flexibility, but it does not eliminate the need to choose between competing uses of capital.
Aramco faces political choices because it is linked to the Kingdom’s public finances. Saudi’s revised government projection puts the 2026 fiscal deficit at SAR245 billion ($65 billion), or 4.9% of GDP. Originally, it was expected to be SAR165 billion. Government spending currently exceeds the original budget by 9.3%, outpacing the upward revision to revenue. For 2027, expenditure is projected at SAR1.392 trillion, while revenues are expected to be SAR1.202 trillion. This comes as the Saudi economy is expected to contract in 2026 by 3.6%. Overall oil activities are expected to fall 21.8%, despite continued growth in non-oil activities. These are government forecasts, which clearly undermine any suggestion that higher oil prices automatically translate into national economic strength.
The oil giant is currently operating under two financial tests. First, the corporate test, which assesses investment returns, operating costs, and cash generation. Second, a sovereign test that concerns the funds required to sustain government spending and economic transformation. It needs to be clear that the Kingdom’s fiscal needs cannot be reduced to Aramco’s production cost per barrel. Even a very profitable producer can still face pressure if its controlling shareholder (the Kingdom/PIF) requires more cash than the business can comfortably distribute over the cycle.
Even if not all Aramco dividends flow directly into the central budget, the coming period's wider Saudi public-sector dependence on oil-generated cash will make dividend restraint politically consequential.
Operational figures show that liquids output fell sharply year on year. At the same time, the NOC said supply reliability fell to 97.8%, down from 99.9% a year earlier. Between the lines, this means a high delivery rate under difficult conditions. However, global customers assess reliability through actual cargo availability, replacement costs, and refinery scheduling. Aramco’s profitability is not their concern.
Geography is also playing an increasingly pivotal role, as the East-West Pipeline remains strategically indispensable. However, the pipeline is no longer an invulnerable escape route. Another geographical distinction is at play. Yanbu exports heading north toward Suez do not need to transit Bab el-Mandeb. Cargoes heading south toward Asian markets generally do. Red Sea exports are now constrained by destination, vessel availability, and the threat environment. Amin Nasser’s statement, “we continue to explore additional overseas storage capacity and alternative export routes,” is a strong and important strategic signal. Aramco will put oil closer to customers while expanding delivery options beyond the current system. This will be more than extra tank capacity; it will also require dependable terminal access, loading and unloading slots, suitable vessel draft, blending facilities, onward pipelines, and contractual rights that remain usable during disruptions. A terminal, tank, or port without a secure supply is not an asset.
Still, keep in mind that overseas storage volumes only buy time. Storage can bridge a disruption only until stocks are depleted. Filling tanks will tie up working capital. Reserve capacity is also costly. Realistic options for all will be European Mediterranean and ARA facilities, or Asian storage.
At the same time, there will be a “Day-After” Hormuz moment, where Aramco will face competing supply. New non-Gulf supply is being developed worldwide. The EIA’s October outlook forecasts US crude production averaging 13.9 million barrels per day in 2026 and 14.3 million in 2027. Other volumes will come from new offshore capacity in Brazil and Guyana, with Guyana increasingly selling into Asian markets. All these grades will be influencing refinery purchasing and bargaining power in Asia.
In the coming years, competition will play a major role, as it is linked to delivered value: crude quality, price, freight, insurance, financing, and dependable arrival. Aramco’s upstream cost advantage remains important, but customers buy delivered cargoes. Persistent uncertainty can encourage diversification even when Saudi production itself remains highly competitive.
At the same time, renewed focus is needed on capital allocation, which is becoming more complex precisely now. Aramco’s 49% HUMAIN investment involves asset transfers and approximately $2.6 billion in cash contributions. At the same time, a mining joint venture adds another adjacent activity. While the media is buzzing about AI, including at ADIPEC 2026, many expect Industrial AI to improve operating performance. At present, these investments still need to demonstrate returns amid competing demands for gas development, export resilience, and shareholder cash.

articles.title_orig: Apple starts giving Siri AI access to third-party apps
articles.title_zh: Apple starts giving Siri AI access to third-party apps
articles.content_orig:
Siri AI will soon be able to carry out tasks across a wider range of apps.
Siri AI will soon be able to carry out tasks across a wider range of apps.
Apple will now let Siri AI perform actions across third-party apps. As part of the iOS 27.3 update rolling out on Tuesday, Apple announced developers can now integrate Siri AI’s new features in “all apps,” allowing the voice assistant to draw on a user’s personal context, process natural language prompts, and use on-screen awareness to complete requests.
The update, which is rolling out as part of a Developer Preview, also adds a new “app skills” feature that third-party developers can create to combine several tasks into a single action. In Apple’s developer documentation , the company says users won’t have to mention an app’s name in their request while it’s in the foreground, during a Live Activity, or in a conversation with Siri AI about the app.
“For example, a person might request a ride with a ride share app, follow updates to the app’s Live Activity while they wait for their ride to arrive, then request to move the pickup location to a different address by saying ‘Hey Siri, change my ride pickup to a new address,’” Apple says. As noted by 9to5Mac , Apple previously made a smaller set of features available to third-party developers.
Apple is bringing Siri AI’s expanded capabilities to its own apps as well, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather apps. “Users can do things like find a coffee shop they visited last week or archive files that haven’t been opened in over a year,” according to Apple. The company notes that users can ask Siri AI what it can do in each app.

articles.title_orig: JetBlue raises bag fees for third time in a year as fuel costs bite
articles.title_zh: JetBlue raises bag fees for third time in a year as fuel costs bite
articles.content_orig:
Welcome to the era of the $70 bag fee.
JetBlue Airways has raised the price of checking a bag for many customers for the third time in less than a year as high fuel costs continue to eat into the industry's profits.
Checking a first bag for travelers booked in economy will now be $50, up from $45, if purchased more than 24 hours before departure during a nonpeak travel period. If it's paid within 24 hours of departure, the fee will be $60. During a peak period, such as during the holidays or the summer, it will be $55 if purchased more than 24 hours before departure, up from $49, and $70 for within 24 hours of departure.
There are exceptions to the checked bag fees, such as for customers who hold a co-branded JetBlue credit card or who hold elite frequent flyer status.
"We're adjusting checked bag fees to help offset rising fuel and operating costs," JetBlue said in a statement. "This helps us keep our base fares competitive while giving customers the choice to pay for a checked bag only if they need one."
The price of jet fuel, airlines' biggest cost after labor, has roughly doubled this year since the start of the Iran war in February, costing airlines billions and driving up the price of tickets. Jet fuel was going for $4.44 a gallon on Tuesday for the U.S. Gulf of Mexico, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
Other airlines often follow when one carrier raises fees. Major U.S. airlines did so earlier this year after JetBlue raised its bag fees.
The changes were reported earlier by the Thrifty Traveler blog .

articles.title_orig: This Election Day, remember which party ran against EVs and tethered us all to the gas pump
articles.title_zh: This Election Day, remember which party ran against EVs and tethered us all to the gas pump
articles.content_orig:
Donald Trump and congressional Republicans spent years waging a culture war against EVs. Now, record gas prices and a foreign war are leaving voters stuck footing the bill at the pump.
Donald Trump and congressional Republicans spent years waging a culture war against EVs. Now, record gas prices and a foreign war are leaving voters stuck footing the bill at the pump.
It’s the midterms! Here’s a fun fact for you as you head to the polls: Gas prices today are the highest ever recorded for a US Election Day.
The national average for a gallon of gasoline is $4.12 and $6.28 for a gallon of diesel, according to GasBuddy. Meanwhile, the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which is maintained by the US Department of Energy as a safeguard during energy crises, is down to 282.2 million barrels of crude, the lowest level in 44 years .
Gas prices, along with other essential cost-of-living items, are certainly top of mind for many voters this election cycle. And perhaps many will also remember which political party ran on a campaign message of ending the fictional “EV mandate” and “drill, baby, drill.”
For the past two years, Donald Trump and congressional Republicans have made gutting EV incentives , freezing charging infrastructure funding , and rolling back fuel economy standards a hallmark of their tenure in power. As a result, EV sales plummeted in the US, ensuring that Americans would stay indefinitely shackled to fossil fuels for years to come. For Trump, it was fulfilling a promise he made during the 2024 campaign. And for his donors from the oil and gas industry, it was money well spent .
Most voters might not have cared that much. After all, skepticism toward EVs was already high, driven by premium prices and lingering charging anxiety. But when Trump went to war with Iran, the resulting surge in gas prices sent Americans scrambling for cheaper ways to get around. Many turned to hybrid and electric vehicles as a solution — only to find vehicle prices were still higher than average, with no federal incentive to help defray the costs. Dealerships saw a surge of foot traffic from drivers who were skeptical of battery-powered cars, now desperate for anything that ran on a plug or a hybrid motor.
While automakers had made strides toward cheaper EVs, the average transaction price still hovered well over $50,000. But the incentive that once helped close that gap — the $7,500 federal clean vehicle tax credit, applied instantly at the point of sale — was gone. The subsidies had been systematically dismantled or left to lapse under the banner of fiscal discipline and anti-green populism.
Here is the real irony of this election. Republicans spent years painting electric cars as an out-of-touch, liberal fad, doing everything they could to kill tax credits and charging programs. They rolled back fuel economy standards that would have forced automakers to build more fuel-efficient powertrains, claiming they were saving everyday drivers from expensive technology they didn’t want.
Instead, they took away an important tool that could have protected family budgets from a global energy crisis. Electricity is made right here at home; its price doesn’t spike every time conflict breaks out in the Middle East. But because Republicans treated EVs like a partisan culture war, millions of Americans are stuck standing at the pump, watching the price roll higher.
Even if Democrats win back Congress, don’t expect them to bring back the Biden-era EV tax credits. The political fight over what kind of car people drive is probably stuck. At the same time, major car companies are backing Trump’s push in court to roll back strict fuel-economy rules. Electric cars aren’t disappearing, but they now have to stand on their own two feet. Companies like General Motors and Ford do have plans to make them more affordable, as long as the government keeps blocking cheap Chinese models from entering the market.
In the end, Trump won his culture war against the electric car. Automakers retreated, subsidies vanished, and the traditional combustion engine was saved from the bureaucrats. But victories have price tags. And as voters step into the booth with a $4 gallon of gas on their minds, they might finally realize what was traded away: the simple freedom to drive past the pump and never look back.

An MSC cruise was canceled after the Coast Guard detained the ship at PortMiami. NBC6’s Isabella Martinez reports
A cruise ship was detained at PortMiami by the U.S. Coast Guard on Sunday, as officials verify its "compliance with international standards and U.S. regulations," according to a statement.
The MSC Poesia was detained during an "expanded examination of the vessel," the U.S. Coast Guard Southeast District said.
